# Audio direction — the Bonelight sound contract

Decided 2026-09-05, alongside the first complete SFX set. This file is to sound what
`.ai/art-direction.md` is to pixels: the format, the element palette, the mix, the frequency
budget, the engine settings, and the rules that keep sixty-nine sounds behaving like one
system. Read it before adding, retuning or wiring any sound.

`.ai/audio-manifest.md` lists every file and where it is meant to be triggered. This file
says *why* each one sounds the way it does.

**The one-line version:** every sound is generated by code in `tools/audio/`, never recorded
or hand-edited; the first 8 ms of every element sound is the same white transient so a cast
always reads as "a spell went off"; and a sound's loudness is set by how *often* it plays,
not by how important it feels.

## 1. Why the set is synthesised

Three hard constraints, in the order they bind:

- This machine has **Python 2.7 with PIL and nothing else** — no numpy, no ffmpeg, no
  ImageMagick, no audio encoder, no virtualenv. `tools/art/` already works under exactly that
  constraint, and `tools/audio/` follows it.
- There is **no audio model in the loop**. Nothing in this pipeline can render a description
  into a recording. What it can do is oscillators, envelopes, filters and saturation, which
  is the sfxr/Bfxr vocabulary and a natural fit for a pixel-art roguelite.
- **No one working on this project can hear the files by reading the source.** That is why
  `tools/audio/analyse.py` exists and why section 8 is a measurement, not an assertion.

The consequence is a boundary worth stating plainly: this pipeline produces synthetic,
retro-adjacent effects. It cannot produce voice, foley, recorded impacts, or music. The two
music tracks in `assets/` stay as they are — see `.ai/decisions/2026-09-05-procedural-sfx.md`.

## 2. Format

| Property | Value | Why it is not negotiable |
|---|---|---|
| Channels | **mono** | `AudioStreamPlayer2D` will not pan a stereo stream, and nearly every gameplay sound in this game is positional. Stereo throws away the only spatial cue a top-down swarm has. |
| Sample rate | 44100 Hz | Godot's WAV importer resamples anything else. |
| Bit depth | 16-bit PCM | The importer's native format; no decode cost at play time. |
| Container | `.wav` | There is no OGG encoder on this machine. WAV is also the only format Godot will loop sample-accurately. |
| Location | `assets/sfx/`, flat | One directory, prefix-sorted names. No per-category subdirectories. |
| Fades | 0.4 ms in, 6 ms out, applied **before** normalising | A buffer that starts or ends off zero is a click, and a click at swarm rates is a buzz. A fade applied *after* normalising attenuates the transient the mix target was measured against — that bug cost four sounds up to 9 dB of attack before it was caught. |

Loop sounds are the one exception: they are **not** faded, because on a loop the fade *is*
the click. See `spell_beam_loop` in `tools/audio/sfx.py` for how a seamless loop is built.

## 3. The pipeline

```
tools/audio/synth.py    oscillators, envelopes, filters, saturation, reverb, WAV writer
tools/audio/palette.py  the twelve element voices + the shared transient
tools/audio/sfx.py      one function per named sound, plus REGISTRY
tools/audio/build.py    writes assets/sfx/, reports levels, flags problems
tools/audio/analyse.py  the distinctness audit (section 8)
```

```
python tools/audio/build.py                 # write the whole set (about 90 s)
python tools/audio/build.py cast_ impact_   # only names containing these
python tools/audio/build.py --preview       # also write per-category audition reels
python tools/audio/build.py --manifest      # print the markdown table for the manifest doc
python tools/audio/analyse.py --confuse     # the distinctness audit
```

**The generators are the source; the `.wav` files are output.** Never hand-edit a file in
`assets/sfx/` — edit the builder and re-run, exactly as with `tools/art/`. Every random draw
comes from a seeded `random.Random`, so a rebuild is byte-identical; if two runs differ,
something has introduced time- or address-dependent randomness and that is a bug.

`tools/audio/_preview_<category>.wav` are audition reels — every sound in a category with
250 ms gaps. They are working files: nothing loads them and they are not shipped.

## 4. The element palette

`.ai/art-direction.md` §3 states the visual rule for the twelve elements:

> The core of every element's effect is white-hot. Identity lives in the mid and edge.

This is the same rule in time:

> **The first 8 ms of every element sound is the same white transient. Identity lives in the
> body and the tail.**

So a cast reads as "a spell went off" on the attack, and *which* element answers a beat
later. The transient is the audio equivalent of the reserved rim colour: shared, bright, and
never element-tinted. One drawn burst serves every element by remapping its ramp; one
transient serves every element by prefixing its body.

The numbers live in `ELEMENTS` in `tools/audio/palette.py` — that dict is the source of
truth and this table is its description. Rows are ordered to match the colour table in the
art contract. Centroid is measured by `analyse.py`, not authored.

| Element | Character | Body | Centroid |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fire | roaring, gritty, low | irregularly gated bandpassed noise sweeping 1400→200 Hz over a sine thump, heavily saturated | 3.9 kHz |
| Ice | brittle, glassy, high | inharmonic partials (1 : 2.76 : 5.40 : 8.93) rising slightly, plus a frost hiss | 6.7 kHz |
| Arcane | shimmering, tonal, rising | two triangles detuned 0.7%, tremolo at 17 Hz, filter opening 2000→4200 Hz | 5.8 kHz |
| Darkness | swelling, sub-heavy, airless | a saw + almost no noise, built forwards then **reversed** so it arrives instead of decaying | 4.0 kHz |
| Light | bell, sustained, warm-bright | a struck bell stack on A5 with a fifth under it | 5.3 kHz |
| Grass | woody, short, blunt | a filtered saw pluck with a pitched-noise knock | 2.5 kHz |
| Earth | low thud, rubble | a sine dropping 150→44 Hz plus decimated lowpassed noise | 2.1 kHz |
| Wind | airy, pitchless, no bass | two bandpasses sweeping in opposite directions, highpassed at 520 Hz | 6.7 kHz |
| Lightning | fast, bright, crackling | a 6200→1300 Hz noise zap plus irregularly gated high noise | 10.8 kHz |
| Poison | wet, bubbling, mid-band | 9 Hz FM gurgle through a narrow bandpass, with gated blips | 4.4 kHz |
| Metal | struck, ringing, inharmonic | six inharmonic partials (1 : 1.71 : 2.46 : 3.39 : 4.51 : 5.88), ring-modulated at 137 Hz | 3.6 kHz |
| Water | droplet, dark wash | a fast rising droplet over a heavily lowpassed wash held at 0.34 gain | 5.6 kHz |

Each element ships two files: `cast_<element>.wav` and `impact_<element>.wav`.

**The impact is not a quieter cast.** Impacts fire far more often — one cast can produce a
dozen — so `palette.impact()` squeezes the body to 55%, adds a low thump, cuts the reverb to
60%, and lands 4 dB under the cast. Darkness additionally plays *forwards* at impact length:
the reversal is a cast gesture, and an impact has already arrived.

**A new element means a new row in `ELEMENTS`, reviewed, then used.** Never numbers typed
inline at a call site. That is the same budget discipline the colour table is under, and for
the same reason: twelve is already at the edge of what a player can tell apart.

## 5. Loudness is a function of frequency of play

This is the rule the whole mix hangs off, and it is counterintuitive:

> **How loud a sound is depends on how often it plays, not on how important the event is.**

An XP orb is a genuinely important event and it is the quietest file in the game, because a
run collects thousands of them. A boss death is the loudest, because it happens once.

Targets are peak dBFS, set per entry in `REGISTRY` in `tools/audio/sfx.py`. `build.py`
normalises every file to its target, so **the registry *is* the mix**: the game plays these
at unity and balance is changed by editing one number and re-running, not by hunting
`VolumeDb` overrides across forty call sites.

| Band | Peak target | Typical members |
|---|---|---|
| Once a run | −3 to −5 dBFS | `boss_death`, `player_death`, `stage_clear`, `meta_unlock`, `spell_evolve`, `level_up` |
| Once a minute | −6 to −9 dBFS | `chest_open`, `player_hurt`, `elite_spawn`, `spell_explosion`, `card_select` |
| Once a second | −11 to −15 dBFS | casts, `enemy_death_*`, `enemy_shoot`, most of `ui_*` |
| Many times a second | −17 to −22 dBFS | `impact_*` (−13), `enemy_hurt_*` (−17), `spell_orbit` (−20), `pickup_xp` (−22) |
| Subliminal | −24 dBFS | `ui_hover` — it plays on every mouse movement across a button |

`pickup_xp` sits 19 dB under `boss_death`. That gap is deliberate and it is what stops a
level-3 Arcane build from turning into white noise.

## 6. The frequency budget

Only one thing may own each band at a time, or a dense screen turns to mud:

- **Sub, below 80 Hz** — `spell_explosion`, `boss_death`, `boss_roar`, `earth`. Nothing else
  may put energy here. A swarm sound with a sub component is the fastest way to lose the mix.
- **Low, 80–300 Hz** — `player_hurt`, `enemy_death_heavy`, the thumps under impacts.
- **Mid, 300 Hz–2 kHz** — the music lives here. Gameplay sounds cross it briefly and leave.
- **High-mid, 2–8 kHz** — where most element identity sits, and where the ear is most
  sensitive. The most contested band in the game; check anything new against a busy screen.
- **Top, above 8 kHz** — `lightning`, `ice`, `ui_hover`, `card_appear`, the shared transient.
  Cheap to occupy because the music barely reaches it.

## 7. Variation at play time, not on disk

Repetition fatigue is solved in the engine, not by generating more files:

- **Pitch.** Randomise `AudioStreamPlayer2D.PitchScale` in roughly `0.94–1.06` on every
  frequently-repeating one-shot. `pickup_xp` should additionally ramp its pitch **upward**
  with the collection streak and reset when the streak breaks — one file, an entire ladder.
- **Variants.** Only three sounds ship variants (`enemy_hurt_a/b/c`), because only they
  repeat fast enough to machine-gun. They differ by seed and by a few Hz, never by intent;
  the audit declares them as twins rather than flagging them.
- **Rate limiting.** `enemy_hurt_*` and `impact_*` must be throttled at the call site — one
  per ~60 ms across all enemies, not one per hit. An AoE landing on forty enemies must play
  one impact, not forty.
- **Voice cap.** Godot has a global limit on simultaneous streams; hitting it drops sounds
  arbitrarily, including important ones. Cap the swarm-rate categories yourself so the
  budget is spent on things the player needs to hear.

## 8. The audit — measure distinctness, do not assert it

`.ai/art-direction.md` §4 does not claim the enemy silhouettes are distinct; it measures the
overlap and reports 1.00 for the two that are the same sprite. `tools/audio/analyse.py` is
that audit for sound:

```
python tools/audio/analyse.py --confuse
```

It reports spectral centroid, 85% rolloff, spread, attack time and crest factor for every
sound, then the pairwise cosine distance between **profiles** — 24 log-spaced spectral bands
plus 12 envelope bands. The envelope half is load-bearing: on spectrum alone, `reroll`
measured as a near-twin of `ui_click`, which it literally is — five copies of it spread over
200 ms. Shape over time is to sound what silhouette is to a sprite.

**Anything at or below 0.10 is confusable and must be fixed or declared.** The current set
measures **0 confusable pairs**, with the three declared twins listed in `TWINS`. Nine real
collisions were found and fixed on the way there, and they are the useful part of the
record because they are the mistakes this palette invites. The last three surfaced only
once the envelope term was added to the metric, which is itself the argument for having it.

| Pair | Was | Why it collided | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cast_arcane` / `cast_water` | 0.041 | both mid-band tonal sweeps over a noise bed | arcane moved up an octave; water’s wash cut to 0.34 gain and the droplet made dominant |
| `cast_fire` / `cast_wind` | 0.058 | both are just wide-band noise under an envelope | fire pushed down to 1400→200 Hz with a stronger thump; wind highpassed at 520 Hz, because air has no bass |
| `stage_clear` / `meta_unlock` | 0.029 | two ascending bell arpeggios in one register | `meta_unlock` rebuilt as a sustained stacked-fifths swell — a swelling chord against a struck one |
| `elite_spawn` / `boss_roar` | 0.082 | an elite shared a boss’s register | `elite_spawn` rebuilt as a reversed struck-metal tone an octave and a half up |
| `card_appear` / `ui_open` | 0.039 | both whoosh-plus-bell, played 400 ms apart | `card_appear` stripped to a pure high-band paper flick with no pitched component |
| `chest_open` / `pickup_health` | 0.094 | every reward in the game was a bell | `pickup_health` rebuilt as a soft filtered sine glow, so HP owns its own timbre |
| `impact_darkness` / `impact_wind` | 0.092 | reversing a swell and then applying `impact()`’s decay leaves a shapeless blob | darkness plays **forwards** below 0.4 s — the reversal is a cast gesture, and an impact has already arrived |
| `pickup_health` / `pickup_magnet` | 0.078 | two smooth rising tonal glides | `pickup_magnet` rebuilt as six accelerating blips, because the event is many orbs arriving |
| `level_up` / `spell_evolve` | 0.089 | both led with the same bell arpeggio, and they fire seconds apart | `spell_evolve` reordered swell-first, bells last — a transformation with a result, not a second level |

The lesson generalises: **collisions happen between sounds built from the same construct**,
and the fix is almost always to change the construct rather than to nudge a frequency.

## 8b. The mix audit - what forty of them at once sounds like

`analyse.py` answers "can these two sounds be told apart". It cannot answer the question that
decides whether a game sounds good: **when forty of them fire at once, can you still hear the
one that matters.** `tools/audio/mixsim.py` answers that one.

```
python tools/audio/mixsim.py                     # every scenario, both policies
python tools/audio/mixsim.py --scenario lategame # the worst case
```

It replays a synthetic minute of a run - hit rates ramping with wave pressure, spells on their
cooldowns, a boss roar partway through - through a model of `SfxPlayer`, mixes the result,
writes a `.wav` you can listen to, and reports peak, crest factor, clipping, and the number the
exercise exists for: **headroom**, per critical event, meaning how far that boss roar rose above
the swarm already playing. Below about 6 dB a sound is present but not noticed; below 3 dB it
may as well not have played.

**The model is parsed, not copied.** Voice counts and throttle windows are read out of
`scripts/SfxPlayer.cs` at run time, and the simulator refuses to start if a constant it expects
has been renamed. A simulator that quietly stops matching the runtime is worse than none,
because it launders a guess into a measurement.

It approximates Godot 2D attenuation as `(1 - d/max)` and does not model the music bus, reverb
interaction between voices, or the listener. Good enough to rank two policies against each
other; not a mastering tool.

### What the first run found

| Finding | Evidence | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **The mix clips in every scenario, including the sparse early game** | peak +1.5 to +2.5 dBFS, 81-234 clipped samples | The registry levels were each set in isolation and nothing had measured their sum. A limiter at -1 dBFS fixes it for 2.5 dB of crest factor. |
| **A tiered priority policy is worth 5-8 dB** on critical sounds | worst critical headroom +3.6 dB to +12.1 dB; voice steals 215 to 35 in the late game | Validated in simulation, not yet implemented. |
| **`elite_spawn` cannot cut through a late-game swarm** | -20.5 dB under the swarm, still -10.3 dB after ducking and ignoring distance | Not a mix problem. It is a rising swell, and a swell has no transient to punch through noise with. It needs redrawing in `sfx.py`, not more gain. |
| Throttling already discards a third of all events | 1954 of 5107 suppressed in the late game | Existing behaviour, now visible. |

The third row is the useful shape of this tool: it turns "that does not cut through" from an
opinion into a number, and points at the generator rather than the mixer.

## 8c. Priority and ducking

Two axes that feel like one knob and are not. Conflating them is the mistake this section
exists to prevent.

- **Priority** decides who wins when voices run out. Every sound has one.
- **Duck authority** decides who makes other sounds quieter. Almost nothing has it.

`SfxCatalog.SfxTier` declares three tiers, and `RegressionChecks` warns if more than fourteen
sounds are Critical, because the mechanism only works while Critical is rare.

| Tier | Members | When voices run out | Distance | Ducks others |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Swarm` | `enemy_hurt_*`, all `impact_*`, `pickup_xp`, `spell_orbit` | **drops itself** - never steals | attenuated | no |
| `Normal` | casts, enemy deaths, UI, pickups, chest | steals a Swarm voice, else drops | attenuated | no |
| `Critical` | the ten rare, run-defining sounds | steals Swarm then Normal; never stolen | **ignored** | yes |

**`player_hurt` is not Critical**, despite being loud and important. While the player is being
swarmed it fires several times a second, and a duck that retriggers before it releases turns
the mix into a pump and removes hit feedback at the exact moment the player is dying.

**Criticals ignore distance attenuation.** `mixsim` measured `elite_spawn` at 20 dB *under* the
swarm purely because it happened to spawn across the screen. A rule that says "this is the
sound that matters" and then halves it for being 380 px away is not a rule. They keep their
position, so they still pan.

### The bus tree

```
Master
├── Music
└── SFX            <- the player volume slider, plus one AudioEffectHardLimiter at -1 dBFS
    ├── SFX_Bed       <- everything Normal and Swarm; this is the bus the duck lowers
    └── SFX_Priority  <- Critical only; never ducked
```

The split exists so the duck can never fight the volume slider. If both lived on one bus, the
duck would overwrite whatever the player had just set - and a critical sound would duck itself.

The duck is **scripted, not sidechained**. Godot does have `AudioEffectCompressor.Sidechain`
and it would sound more organic, but a fixed curve is exactly reproducible inside
`tools/audio/mixsim.py` and a compressor is not. While nobody on this project can hear the
difference to referee it, predictable beats organic.

`DuckDb` is -6 dB and `DuckReleaseSeconds` is 0.30, both in `SfxPlayer` - and `mixsim` parses
them out of that file rather than keeping its own copy. It deliberately does not duck to
silence: losing hit feedback during a boss roar is worse than the noise it was fixing.

## 9. Godot integration

`.ai/audio-manifest.md` holds the wiring table and what remains. What exists now:

- **Buses.** `default_bus_layout.tres` defines Master, Music, SFX and SFX's two children
  (see the tree in section 8c), with an `AudioEffectHardLimiter` at -1 dBFS on SFX.
  `MusicPlayer` and `SfxPlayer` resolve every bus by name with a fallback one level up, and
  `RegressionChecks` warns for each missing bus and for a missing limiter - all three
  fallbacks are silent, and one of them was a shipped bug before the layout existed.
- **Positional vs global.** Anything with a world position — casts, impacts, enemy sounds —
  uses `AudioStreamPlayer2D`. UI, stingers and `player_*` use plain `AudioStreamPlayer`.
- **Import settings.** Godot's WAV importer defaults are correct for everything here, with
  one exception already applied: `assets/sfx/spell_beam_loop.wav.import` carries
  `edit/loop_mode=1` (Forward). That setting lives in the `.import` file, not the WAV, so
  **regenerating the file keeps it but deleting the `.import` loses it**. Note also that the
  importer defaults to `compress/mode=2`, which is QOA — lossy. That is the right trade for
  short effects; if an artefact ever shows up on the quietest files, PCM is `compress/mode=0`.
- **`tools/audio/` carries a `.gdignore`.** Nothing in there is loaded by the game, and
  without it Godot imports several megabytes of audition reel into `.godot/`.
- **Preloading and pooling.** `SfxPlayer` loads all 69 streams in `_Ready` and plays them
  through a fixed pool of 24 positional and 8 non-positional voices. Never call
  `ResourceLoader.Load` or `new AudioStreamPlayer2D()` on a frame the game is running.
- **Persistence.** Volumes live in `SaveData` as linear 0..1 and are applied by
  `AudioSettings.ApplyFromSave` from `SfxPlayer._Ready`, which runs after `SaveManager`
  because of the autoload order in `project.godot`.

## 10. Adding a sound

1. Write a builder in `tools/audio/sfx.py`. Compose from `synth.py` primitives; if it is
   elemental, go through `palette.body()` rather than typing new numbers.
2. Add it to `REGISTRY` with a category, a peak target chosen from the table in §5, and the
   loop flag. **A function that is not in the registry does not ship** — `build.py` does not
   scan the module.
3. `python tools/audio/build.py <name>` and check the report: it must hit its target exactly,
   and must not be flagged as clipped, long or under target.
4. `python tools/audio/analyse.py --confuse` and confirm it did not land within 0.10 of an
   existing sound in its category. If it did, change the construct, not the gain.
5. Add its row to `.ai/audio-manifest.md` with the intended trigger site.
6. Commit the generator change **and** the regenerated `.wav`.

## Don't

- Hand-edit a `.wav` in `assets/sfx/`. Edit the builder and re-run.
- Ship stereo. It costs positional audio and nothing here needs it.
- Fade a loop, or fade anything after normalising.
- Use the module-level `random` anywhere in `tools/audio/`. Seeded instances only, or the
  build stops being reproducible.
- Add a variant file to fix repetition. Randomise `PitchScale` first; variants are a last
  resort and currently exist for exactly one sound.
- Give a swarm-rate sound a sub component, a reverb tail, or a length over ~200 ms.
- Set loudness by how important the event feels. Set it by how often it fires.
- Add a thirteenth element voice without adding its row to `ELEMENTS` and re-running the
  confusion audit.
